title: Why we Should Study Solitary Species to Understand the Costs of Group‐Living
content:
It's easier to measure the benefits than the costs of a trait. Solitary species benefit by avoiding the costs of group living. Thus, measuring benefits of solitary living informs us about the costs of group living.


ABSTRACT

While for decades behavioral ecologists have studied the benefits of group living, measuring its costs has been more difficult. It is generally easier to measure the benefits of a trait than its costs, because for the trait to have evolved the benefits must be higher than the costs, leading to a net benefit. Importantly, the benefits of solitary living are avoiding the costs of group living, such as transmission of disease and competition for resources and reproduction. Consequently, measuring the benefits of solitary living provides a way to quantify the costs of group living. Alternatively, we can ask: What would be the benefits for group-living individuals to switch to solitary living to avoid the costs of group living? And: What would be the costs of solitary living individuals becoming group-living? To answer these questions, we suggest studying species that show intra-specific variation in social organization, which means sometimes they live solitary, sometimes in pairs or groups. We can then compare parasite load, predation risk, reproductive competition and access to resources between solitary and group-living individuals of the same species in the same environment, and ultimately compare outcomes of solitary versus group-living for growth, survival and reproduction.
